Messages.Author: Hyllan
Messages.Body:
My impression of this year's EC was that combat decks, or decks
splashed with combat, was more common than the previous two years. Aim
cards were the major change. It is not a bad thing that combat is
getting easier to oust with; Dragonbound, Frontal Assault and Hell-for-
Leather are nice examples, though Dragonbound has been around for a
while now. It's also a valid argument that non-combat decks should be
forced to include some sort of combat defense, like fortitude or S:CE.
But I'm not sure if the aim cards are balanced anyway.

Target Vitals sees much more play than the other ones. Sure, it's
uncommon, not a rare, but it's also better than the other ones. If not
canceled, Target Head is stronger, but it only takes 1 card to cancel
it. It's like Perfectionist compared to Capitalist. Wouldn't it have
been better if Target Vitals was cancelled by one card as well?

And why weren't the aim cards designed to require disciplines? Auspex
or Celerity, for example. Did Imbued and 1-caps need to get better at
combat?

Target Hand, Combat, R , [LotN]

Aim. Play when choosing a strike.The opposing minion may discard two
combat cards to cancel this card. If any damage from this strike is
successfully inflicted on the opposing minion, he or she gets -1
strength this action, and you may destroy a weapon he or she has. A
minion may play only one aim each strike.

Target Head, Combat, R , [LotN]

Aim. Play when choosing a strike.The strike does +2 damage. The
opposing minion may discard a combat card to cancel this card. If any
damage from this strike is successfully inflicted on the opposing
minion, he or she cannot use any additional strikes or presses this
round, and you may set the range for the next round. A minion may play
only one aim each strike.

Target Leg, Combat, R , [LotN]

Aim. Play when choosing a strike.The opposing minion may discard two
combat cards to cancel this card. If any damage from this strike is
successfully inflicted on the opposing minion, he or she may use
maneuvers or presses only if they require Obfuscate [obf] ,
Thaumaturgy [tha] or Flight this action. A minion may play only one
aim each strike.

Target Vitals, Combat, U , [LotN]

Aim. Play when choosing a strike.If any damage from this strike is
successfully inflicted on the opposing minion, he or she takes an
additional 2 damage from this strike, and he or she cannot press this
round. The opposing minion may discard two combat cards to cancel this
card. A minion may play only one aim each strike.

TV is not a strike, so comparing it to strike cards can be a little
off. Sure, if you're only going to play either LB or TV, TV is better
against everything except Flak Jackets and other 'prevent one'. But
you can play both LB and TV on one strike, so they aren't really in

On Sep 25, 7:52 am, Hyllan <caroline_h...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> Target Vitals sees much more play than the other ones.

It is clearly the best of them. Although in a combat heavy
environment, it rarely works (as it is easily foiled by dodge, S:CE, 1
point of prevention, or discarding 2 combat cards) the way you hope it
will (I was playing multiple TVs in all sorts of decks for a while
locally, and in the end, they rarely ever paid off, so I swapped them
out for things that are more generally effective). In a low combat
environment, it can be a total killer. But if folks have, like, a
manuver or a Flak Jacket, the huge pile of Target Vitals as combat
offense isn't going to help all that much.

Target Head isn't horrible, as it increases your strike's base damage,
so it isn't foiled by a single point of damage prevention. But it *is*
foiled by a single combat card discard, making that much easier to
avoid. But as it is Rare, Target Vitals generally eclipses it. The
other two Targets are kind of janky (although Target Hand isn't bad as
disciplinless anti-weapon tech if you really want some).

> It's like Perfectionist compared to Capitalist. Wouldn't it have
> been better if Target Vitals was cancelled by one card as well?

Probably. Using the bad (i.e. most) Archetypes as comparison isn't
great, as the first batch were *clearly* underpowered, and the second
batch (uh, Perfectionist?) were reasonable. Yeah, the rest of the
Archetypes pretty much blow. But that is ok. Target Vitals is
generally much, much better than the other three, yes. And is possibly
overpowered. But not by much. And it is probably ok that the other
ones are kind of janky.

> Did Imbued and 1-caps need to get better at combat?

Again, Target Vitals *can* be very strong, but generally only in the
context of "My deck has zero combat cards in it..." in which case, it
was getting schooled by any sort of combat offense anyway. But in the
face of any sort of reasonable combat package, a dozen Target Vitals
aren't going to do much.

-Peter

against and gain a blood - not sure it was really worth it to have
like 5 Traditionalists in the deck for that purpose, but it seemed to
help the deck at the time). Which is interesting - other than Monster
and Perfectionist, all of the usable archetypes seem to be trifles. I
thought it would be interesting to build a deck around Conniver at one
point, but the fact that it is not a trifle and is even weaker than
some of the ones that are trifles, *and* the fact that it's not "once

Ya think? Perfectionist seems like a completely reasonable card in and
of itself--an MPA to conditionally gain blood on a single minion, if
their action is successful *and* no reaction is played. Seems like a
totally ok master card. Yeah, it completely makes the other Archetypes
total wallpaper, but that is 'cause they were bad, not 'cause
Perfectionist is too good. The first chunk of Archetypes were totally
under the power curve. Perfectionst came out after them, and was about
as good as Archetypes needed to be.

card. Yeah, it is disciplineless, but it is easy to avoid (dodge,

better replaced by something more reliable. It does do a really good
job of making a non combat heavy environment very vulnerable. Which
means that folks should worry about combat more (as the "hope they
don't have blasters" defense took a hit due to Target Vitals, as now a
disciplineless 1 cap can punch you for 3 if you just stand there and
take it). Which strikes me as a totally good thing.

that Target Vitals is necessarily too strong.

You make good points. I'm willing to agree that Perfectionist and
maybe even Target Vitals are in a reasonable area of the power curve
(though TV is borderline imho). The fact that TV gives all decks
decent hitback ability is probably a good thing, all things
considered.

About the archetypes: yes, the problem is mostly the fact that most of
the others suck in comparison to Perfectionist, adding yet more
wallpaper to the game. Perfectionist as such is a pretty balanced
card, the others (bar Monster, another later addition) mostly suck.
This is annoying, but you're right; the design flaw isn't
Perfectionist as much as the other archetype cards which are too low-
powered.

About the aim cards: there the situation is a bit different. We have
Target Vitals, which is borderline overpowered for a no-discipline
card. Then we have Target Head, which isn't actually all that bad --
only the "discard one card to cancel it" clause makes it less
universally rocking as TV. Onwards to Target Hand, which is actually a
pretty damn strong card in many decks, especially when combined with
Trap. Last of all we have Target Legs, which imho is the only Aim card
which actually sucks. So here the "problem" is the power level of
Target Vitals itself, which can be argued various ways.

So to correct myself: the design team glitches have actually more to
do with

a) the very low power level of the non-Perfectionist archetype cards,
which makes them wallpaper(ish)
b) the power level of Target Vitals, and the suckiness of Target Legs

Or not. The above is my current feel about those card groups, but I'm
willing to be pursuaded to think differently :D

//Petri

Okay, so maybe comparing one of the best disciplineless combat cards
with one of the worst cards in the game and probably one of the top 5
wastes of cardboard in the free world is not productive... But I
think what he was saying is that Target:Vitals is often better than
even something like Undead Strength, especially if played at inferior
potence. The fact that T:V can be combo'd with another strike is hot,
including ranged strikes and the nasty combo with Catatonic Fear.
Denying a press isn't such a big deal, but it's just an added
benefit. T:V has downsides, obviously, compared to a simple strike
for +2 damage that can't be cancelled with a discard or stopped with 2
less points of prevention.

But the fact that there is a pretty close equivalency between a poster
card for a hitty discipline and a non-discipline combat card feels
wrong, somehow. If you had vampires with potence and your only
choices for combat were Undead Strength and Target: Vitals, my
estimation is that you would use some combination of both (mainly
because they combo together). If you had to choose one or the other
to go in a deck with other combat cards, I think it would be a
difficult choice, based on the rest of your deck and your metagame.

I'm *not* saying T:V is broken, or that it's better than all of the
potence options. I think it's at the top of the power curve for
disciplineless cards. I definitely don't think it needed to deny the
opponent the ability to press, not that that's a major part of what
the card does. It doesn't wallpaper the entire Potence discipline or
anything... but I can at least see what Johannes was saying when he
said that it's better than some Potence cards.

I don't know how Perfectionist could even remotely wallpaper Creep
Show. Creep Show is a trifle, Perfectionist is not. Creep Show can
give you up to 5 blood between your untap phases (assuming a couple of
wakes), Perfectionist is limited to 1 (assuming no Madness Network).
Perfectionist gives you a blood when you complete a successful action,
assuming you're not in an extremely wake-happy environment. Creep
Show gives you a blood when someone dodges or ends combat against you,
which can be good because most combat decks gain blood from Taste of
Vitae, and Creep Show covers you in about half of the cases when Taste
of Vitae wouldn't work for you. So Creep Show is helpful for combat
decks (generally not as much as Monster, granted, and kind of a toss-
up with Curmudgeon for blocking decks).

The cost, effect, and utility are completely different between
Perfectionist and Creep Show. And yeah, I think it's a decent card.
Not as good as Perfectionist in most cases, true, but it has decks
that it could excel in, depending on the metagame.

Well, "playtesting" really shouldn't be in doubt. I'm not sure what
the dispute could be about the definition of playtesting. For me,
playtesting is doing whatever activity needs to be done to learn how
well the set has been defined, spot problems, fix them, and test the
fixes. Yes? No? Did I miss something?

I think the question is about what is "enough" playtesting. Every set,
I see distinct, identifiable, fixable problems. I suppose I have no idea
what it's like being a set designer and having my own ideas about what's
appropriate and getting lots of conflicting comments from lots of sources
and having only a few opportunities to change cards and test the changes.
No doubt it's all very challenging and I wouldn't do as good a job as the
current guy does. But if he had more time and more organization,
I have little doubt he could do a much better job and a lot of problems
that look obvious (to me, anyway) wouldn't get out the door. So, in that
sense, there has not been "enough" playtesting.

From the standpoint of White Wolf, I'm sure the picture looks different.
Since they're wanting to get the sets out the door soon enough and within
budget constraints that make these projects profitable, one would assume
they're doing the best they can. The fact that we're getting new sets and
there are no major player revolts - just a few obnoxiously long threads
about specific cards - probably attests to the fact that they're doing
"enough" testing for their purposes.

One of those, "it-is-what-is" situations, I guess.

It's been noted by industry people* and has been my experience as well
that the more a CCG set is playtested, the stronger it gets.

Two reasons. One is that playtesters (correctly) gravitate to
overpowered stuff first and only get around to pointing out coasters
if there's time.

Two is the removal of the fear factor. The less playtested a set is
the more fear that something will slip through the cracks that is
abusive, counter to designer intent, or whatever in some embarrassing
way. Rigorous playtesting doesn't catch everything (nor should it
since discovery is a huge draw to CCGs), but it gives confidence that
the problems will be minimal and that the game can withstand
additional tournament level cards.

* I first saw it talked about when someone was comparing Homelands to
Alliances. The latter had way more playtesting.

So, the point may be that far too many weak/low use cards get made due
to insufficient playtesting. That much of the useful playtesting of
V:TES sets is done after they are published, leading to corrections in
future sets but doing little to help underpowered cards in print.

Could you clarify what you mean by broken here? Broken is usually taken
to mean something game-breaking - Return to Innocence, old Thoughts
Betrayed, and so on.

- Radically overpowered? Not really. It's only one blood a turn.

- Causes you to have to play it or play against it? Well, you certainly
can play it a lot, but you don't have to - many, many decks in the
TWDA without it. You don't have to thwart it, although you can try to
if you want to. It may also be worth noting that weenie Auspex (and
wall decks generally) are often popular, causing some issues.

- Undermines the predator-prey dynamic? No.

- Wildly inappropriate for the game (like Madness or old Monocle)?
Doesn't seem to be.

It is:

- Better than various other cards of the same type, but that can just
indicate that those cards are bad. (e.g. Lost in Crowds is good, and
Stealth Ritus is fairly poor - but that doesn't mean Lost in Crowds is
broken)

- Easy to include in many decks - but so's Blood Doll, The Barrens,
Dreams of the Sphinx, and plenty of other useful cards.

Neither of these means a card is broken - they can just indicate a good
card. If you've printed some bad cards for a particular mechanic, at
some point you just have to cut your losses and run. You can make some
cards better by printing more support around them - this Anarch card
isn't good enough to make it worth playing in isolation, but with some
more Anarch support in this set, it's a possible include - but some
mechanics just don't have that possibility.

The bottom line is that if Perfectionist had never been printed, various
of the archetypes still wouldn't see use outside of draft, hugely corner
case decks, or fun challenges. Master cards are a precious resource,
and there are a huge number of good cards competing for space in any
given deck, and several of the archetypes just don't cut the mustard,
regardless of Perfectionist.

Undead Strength is kind of a basic measuring stick for cards. It
requires a discipline. It does +1 or +2 damage at various levels. It
does not cost blood. It is a nice, solid, reasonable card.

Target Vitals, when compared to Undead Strength does not require a
discipline (which is a plus, but if you are playing a potence based
combat deck, mostly irrelevant). Does +2 damage instead of +1 (POT
Undead Strength strikes me as strictly superior to TV), but the damage
is conditional--it doesn't happen a lot of the time. Which strikes me
as a wash. The press prevention is a minior bonus, but not huge one
way or the other.

If you are building an all pot based combat deck, I could see an
argument for using Target Vitals instead of Undead Strength. But if
you are building an all pot based combat deck, there are probably lots
of other options too, most of which will take the place of Target
Vitals anyway, as if you are building an all pot based combat deck,
you probably weren't going to be using Undead Strength, either (the
viable pot based combat decks I have seen generally revolve around
fortitude prevent/Disarm, Torn Signpost/CEL Blur, or CEL ranged Sewer
Lids. None of which tend to use Undead Strength anyway). It is
possible that one could argue that the existence of TV makes a pure
weenie pot/IG/TS/TV deck pretty good. But not significantly better
than pure weenie pot/IG/TS/PtL or even pure weenie pot/IG/TS/US, due
to the conditionality of Target Vitals.

So claiming that Target Vitals is strictly superior to Undead Strength
is kind of missing context completely.

-Peter

I think this is one of those cases where I want to argue both sides.
One blood a turn is pretty damned strong - I wouldn't just write it
off like that. Perfectionist doesn't guarantee a blood a turn, and
again, it depends on your metagame. But let's assume for sake of
argument that it's 1 blood per turn. Someone mentioned Palatial
Estate already, 2 blood in order to get a blood per turn. Aaron's
Feeding Razor, 1 pool in order to get a blood per turn only when you
hunt. Inbase Discotek and Hunting Grounds - 2 pool in order to gain 1
blood per turn. In some way, Perfectionist is better than all those
cards. It seems like with the archetype cards, they were trying to
put some restrictions on the use of the cards such that you had to be
doing something in tune with the "personality" or your deck in order
to gain a blood. Gurus vote, Capitalists bleed, Curmudgeons block,
Bravos fight, Conniver - well... should've been a trifle... Are these
cards good in and of themselves? You know, I think they were good
enough (most of them). You still see Guru and Capitalist in decks,
but even though they are cornercase better than Perfectionist in the
right situations, in general I think they would be better off swapped
with Perfectionists, even in decks that do those things. If there
were no Perfectionist, I'm confident that those two, at least, would
see much more play. I don't know why they had to be Sabbat-only -
that's certainly annoying. I suppose there are no capitalists in the
Camarilla?

It's not game-breaking. I'm not going to cry in my Cheerios because
Perfectionist is too good. It's obviously better than most of the
other archetypes, and I think that the other archetypes were more in
line with both the power-curve of previous cards and with what I
thought was the intent and flavor of this class of cards, but it
certainly doesn't ruin V:TES. I think at the very least that
Target:Vitals should not have prevented presses (very minor nerf to a
still-strong card), and Perfectionist probably shouldn't have been
printed at all. Perfectionist is a cop-out archetype in the role-
playing game, too. It's like when you go to a job interview and they
ask you what your biggest flaw is - "oh, I'm too much of a
perfectionist. I need to do everything right. oh, and a workaholic
too - I just have to work, work, work, all the time!" Player says,
"my character is a Perfectionist. He doesn't like to fail at
anything." GM says, "I don't think so... your character's new Nature
is Pederast. Care to choose a Demeanor?" I'd have preferred if
they'd chosen a different archetype instead for V:TES. Even Pederast
woulda been better... ;)

Inbase Discotek is generally a poor comparison, much better to think of
the Hungry Coyote. (This is in as much as IDF doesn't see much play,
whereas Hungry Coyote does - compare the relative frequencies of them in
the TWDA, and the age of the appearances, and I think HC is showing
itself to be comfortably ahead.) Yes, the Coyote only affects the
Sabbat - but it affects all of yours, no tapping.

There's not much point comparing cards with cards that just don't see
play if, as I suspect, the reason they don't see play is that they're
not all that good. We could create a dozen cards that weren't as good
as Coyote, and were on a par with cards that don't see much play. But
what's the point of creating cards in that way? The new cards are
unlikely to see much player either.

Note also that there's plenty of good blood gain in other strategies
(requiring either a discipline or a title or whatever else), and there's
Giant's Blood too. Is Perfectionist better than Giant's Blood? I can
see arguments for either or both. But what about compared to Voter
Captivation? VC seems to blow Perfectionist away to me. Concert Tour
or Renewed Vigor both seem stronger. Combat decks have the potentially
very good Taste of Vitae, and Thaumaturgy has Theft of Vitae, which is
still potentially great. (Yeah, simple aggro-poke lucks out a bit here,
but that's no so unusual - it lucks out in a lot of places.)

Much like Taste of Vitae is blood gain for doing what you're already
wanting to do, Perfectionist is a bit like that for the rest of us - do
your thing, get some blood. Of course, the mechanics are radically
different (permanent master, slower, etc. vs potentially large slurp of
a combat card), but it helps the rest of us - in a way that Inbase
Discotek, Frankfurt, godluvvit, doesn't do in quite the same way.

>If there
>were no Perfectionist, I'm confident that those two, at least, would
>see much more play.

Yet there are many decks that don't include Perfectionist either, but
aren't including Capitalist or Guru or whatever else. If these cards
would see play without Perfectionist, but people aren't even playing
Perfectionist in quite a few decks, it seems to be a problem.

> I don't know why they had to be Sabbat-only -
>that's certainly annoying. I suppose there are no capitalists in the
>Camarilla?

This - and the trifle point - I agree with. It's part of what makes
several of them quite weak - expensive, not contributing as much as they
could. With (for example) Hungry Coyote, the Sabbat restriction isn't
so bad because the power level is much higher, so people will build
around it. Much less incentive to do that with a poor card.

I don't disagree that Perfectionist is better than most other archetypes
(Monster is completely different, and there are a couple of situations
where a couple of the others are okay) - but I simply can't see people
stampeding to the other archetypes if Perfectionist vanished, when other
cards are so much better.

>I think at the very least that
>Target:Vitals should not have prevented presses (very minor nerf to a
>still-strong card), and Perfectionist probably shouldn't have been
>printed at all.

Target Vitals not preventing presses, I'm pretty much in line with. I
don't see it as necessary, really. (And change the aimed location, if
that was considered unrealistic - I don't care.)

But I'm really not convinced that Perfectionist is so good that it's
crowding out all these other archetypes which would just burst onto the
scene were it not for Perfectionist.

Lots of cards aren't necessary if you just build a stealth-bleed deck.
If that were the only yard-stick for a playable card, the game would
probably not extend into 3 figures of playable cards. Nice bits of
Obfuscate, a few bits of Obtenebration, Dominate, Presence,
Dementation... you don't need much else.

But a card like Eternal Mask can be good, even when there are other
options available to a given deck or clan.

- You may be able to take advantage of a better / different[0]
discipline spread. Example here, the Setites have ser available at 2
and 3 caps - they don't have obf/pre until you hit 4 and above.

- Having it on one discipline can make other tasks easier. For example,
breed-boon is a popular and potentially powerful mechanic[1], but you
want something to do with the weenies you breed. Waters of Duat lets
you bring out any one discipline card. You could decide to make that
one card Serpentis and play cards such as Temptation and Eternal Mask.
Do you have to? No, obviously not. But this is a potentially
powerful deck-type that doesn't just rely on stealth-bleed, but uses
it in tandem with another strategy.

- The interesting / weird / challenging superior allows you to take
advantage of odd situations, while having a perfectly playable
inferior level. This is a problem with various other cards with
mildly corner-case uses - if you don't have that situation turn up,
the card is dead. Cyclable, usable, playable inferiors, and the
Bloodlines fallback level, often facilitate interesting play.

- Spirit Marionette, to go off on a tangent temporarily from the above
point, is sometimes played with a horde of Dominate weenies. If the
stealing strategy doesn't work, you just turn into a bleed deck. If
the star vampire is pummelled, you turn into a bleed deck. Using the
weeniefication of Serpentis, you could try something similar here, if
you thought you had a good way to exploit the superior.

- Library efficiency. Some players are meticulous about cutting decks
down to 60 cards, others want to cram in 110 cards and are trying to
find room. In either case, a more efficient card might help them out.
Sure, they'll be different decks to yours, but there isn't only one
best deck for each clan.

- Use where stealth and bleed isn't possible. We've had all sorts of
disciplines splashed in semi-random ways before. Who's to say
Serpentis won't get splashed elsewhere later? Or you might be using
Setites without Obf or Pre, but want some bleed power too. Or LSJ
might design a whole clutch of Warrior Setites (POT/PRE/SER) in the
future, and looky here, a card that doesn't suck for them.

[0] Which is to say, it might not be a better crypt for any given
library, but you might well be able to make a competitive library that
goes about things in a different way.

[1] Obviously, different playgroups will find it different - but it's
hard to deny that good breed-boon can be effective, in the right hands.
